source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL
finding: Eigenvectors of the state-graph Laplacian (proto-value functions) define intrinsic rewards. Each reward trains an option (an eigenoption) that moves the agent along one direction of the state space. No external reward is needed.
numbers: Three tabular gridworlds: open room, I-maze, four-room. Q-learning, 100-step episodes, averaged over 100 trials.
limits: Tabular, deterministic, small domains. Needs the graph, or an SR estimate of it.
agent_relevance: The founding method behind SR eigenvectors giving subgoals. It needs a state graph, which our agent only has if the program builds one from its own attempt trace.

source: Machado et al. (2017) Laplacian framework, bottleneck finding
finding: Eigenoptions are not bottleneck options. In the four-room domain the doorways were not the first options found. The fifth eigenoption was the first to end at a doorway. The authors say eigenoptions are often more useful than bottleneck options.
numbers: Fifth eigenoption = first doorway option in the 4-room domain.
quote: Eigenoptions do not necessarily look for bottleneck states
limits: The usefulness claim rests on small tabular tests. It contradicts the simple story that eigenvectors find bottlenecks.
agent_relevance: Our schema idea of discovering subgoals as bottlenecks should not cite eigenoptions as bottleneck finders. Bottleneck detection and eigenoption discovery are different methods.

source: Machado et al. (2017) Laplacian framework, diffusion time
finding: Eigenoptions cut the diffusion time (expected steps for a random walk to go between any two states). Options let the walker cover distance instead of dithering.
numbers: Compared with primitive actions only in the three domains (figures; per-option values not extracted).
limits: Diffusion time is a proxy for exploration, not for reward. Reward tests are sparse and tabular.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap metric for a subgoal library: does adding this subgoal reduce the expected steps between states of the attempt graph.

source: Machado, Rosenbaum, Guo, Liu, Tesauro, Campbell (2018) Eigenoption discovery through the deep successor representation
finding: Eigenoptions can be found from pixels using a learned deep SR instead of the graph. Tested on four Atari games.
numbers: Options useful in 3 of 4 games (Bank Heist, Montezuma's Revenge, Ms. Pac-Man). Ineffective in Freeway. In Montezuma the option end states matched known human-style subgoals.
quote: our algorithm was ineffective in FREEWAY
limits: Greedy myopic option policies. The key pickup subgoal was not found. Avoiding cars needs longer-term planning. Evidence is mostly visitation plots.
agent_relevance: Failure case: subgoals from state-visitation structure miss subgoals that need an object interaction. Do not expect structure alone to find them.

source: Machado, Barreto, Precup, Bowling (2023) Temporal abstraction in RL with the successor representation (JMLR 24)
finding: Argues the SR is a natural base for finding and using options (the ROD cycle). Compares eigenoptions with covering options in four-room.
numbers: Four-room, 10 random tasks, Q-learning (alpha 0.1, gamma 0.9, epsilon 0.05), 1,000-step cap, 50 episodes. As few as 4 eigenoptions sped learning and never hurt in any of the 10 tasks.
limits: Eigenoptions ignore the task reward. With too few options they make some states near-impossible to reach (sink states) and diffusion time gets worse. Tabular tests.
agent_relevance: A small library (about 4) already helps, but a library that is too small can hurt navigation. Keep primitive moves always available.

source: Machado et al. (2023) JMLR, diffusion time comparison
finding: With enough options, eigenoptions give lower diffusion time than covering options. Using the top ten eigenvectors beats using the top eigenvector ten times over. Covering options lower the median diffusion time even with one option.
numbers: Four-room, closed-form options. Average diffusion time is dominated by outliers; median is not.
limits: Closed-form, deterministic, tabular.
agent_relevance: Use several different structural directions, not repeated bottlenecks of one kind. Report the median, not the mean, when judging a subgoal library.

source: Klissarov and Machado (2023) Deep Laplacian-based Options for Temporally-Extended Exploration (DCEO)
finding: Deep covering eigenoptions: a neural network approximates Laplacian eigenfunctions and trains options online from pixels in stochastic tasks.
numbers: Nine rooms, Maze, 2x2 Rubik's cube, MiniWorld, Montezuma's Revenge (Rainbow). 30 seeds. DCEO at least as good as Counts and RND. DIAYN did not improve on the DDQN baseline in Nine rooms. Largest gap in the Maze.
limits: The first version needs a separate option-discovery phase; the online version removes it. Results concern exploration, not general planning.
agent_relevance: The idea scales past tables, but at the cost of training a network. Our agent cannot train, so only the idea (rank states by graph structure) is portable.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Eight LLMs were tested on cognitive-map planning tasks taken from human experiments, including community-structured graphs. Models list edges well but fail to use them to plan. Three failure modes: invented edges, long routes instead of shortest, and loops.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, davinci-003, Bard, Cohere-52B, Claude-1, LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B. Logistic fit: LLM chi2 2357.87, graph 3431.53, condition 2080.04, domain 304.06 (all p<.001); temperature chi2 1.28, p=.53. Shortest path to a state one cluster away: GPT-4 0 of 30 at temperature 0, at most 10% at 0.5 or 1.
quote: LLMs do not have emergent planning capacities
limits: 2023 models, prompts only, no tools. Many cells are 30 repeated runs.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that cluster structure, the thing eigenoptions exploit, is where plain LLM planning breaks. Let code compute the graph and its bottlenecks; the model should not.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval, effect of BFS/DFS instructions
finding: Telling GPT-4 to use breadth-first or depth-first search helped a little on community graphs, but not consistently or monotonically across temperature.
numbers: 30 runs per prompt and temperature. Cluster counting improved with BFS or DFS at temperatures 0 and 0.5, less at 1. Shortest path within a cluster improved at all temperatures (BFS best at 0). Path one cluster away improved only with BFS at 0.5.
limits: High-level algorithm description only, no worked examples. No effect sizes in the text.
agent_relevance: Naming the algorithm in the prompt is weak. Running the algorithm in code is the fix, in line with code-selects.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Recursive decomposition only when the executor fails. A planner splits a failed sub-task, the executor tries the parts, and this repeats to depth dmax. It beat ReAct, plan-and-execute, retry, and Reflexion.
numbers: GPT-3.5. ALFWorld test, dmax 3: ADaPT 71.6 vs ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try-Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5. WebShop: 44.0 vs ReAct 32.0, Reflexion 35.0, LATS 38.0. TextCraft (dmax 4): 52.0 vs ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Reflexion 32.0. Pick2 tasks: baselines under 12%, ADaPT 52.9%.
limits: Needs an executor that can signal failure. Text games and shopping, not open problems.
agent_relevance: Closest match to guardrail G1: decompose only on a failure signal. A subgoal library entry should be created by a failed attempt, not on a schedule.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT, depth and executor strength
finding: Success rises with allowed decomposition depth on all three datasets. ADaPT lifts weak executors the most and holds up as recipe depth grows.
numbers: TextCraft, ADaPT dmax 4: depth-2 recipes 78.2% vs ReAct 26.9%; depth-3 recipes 38.7%. Weak atomic-skill executor on ALFWorld dev: 3.3% to 41.7%. The biggest step is dmax 1 to 2.
limits: More depth means more LLM calls. Dev-split analyses.
agent_relevance: Depth 2 captures most of the gain. Cap recursion at two or three levels in the schema.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: An LLM agent in Minecraft keeps a growing skill library of verified code programs, retrieved by description and reused as building blocks. This is an option library built inside an LLM loop.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA. Removing self-verification cut discovered items by 73%. GPT-4 gave 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5 for code generation.
limits: Needs a game engine for verification. Three runs per tech-tree cell. Skills are written by the LLM, not found by graph structure.
agent_relevance: A working subgoal library inside an LLM loop. The key part is code-verified admission to the library, which fits G2 and G3.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM)
finding: An LLM proposes sensible goals from a text description of the state, and the agent is rewarded for reaching them. This picks goals from language priors instead of from state-graph structure.
numbers: Crafter and Housekeep. In Housekeep, LLM accuracy on some object classes was above 87% but receptacle accuracy ranged 50-90%. Goal conditioning gave no significant gain in pretraining.
quote: the LLM never suggests creating wood pickaxes
limits: A missed goal can never be learned. Prompt-sensitive. Helps less when common sense is irrelevant or the state is not in text.
agent_relevance: The LLM-side alternative to c01: subgoals from priors. Pair with structure-based proposals to cover goals the model never names.

source: Fu et al. (2024) Language-guided Skill Learning with Temporal Variational Inference (LAST)
finding: An LLM segments expert trajectories into pieces. A variational method then merges pieces into reusable skills, with a minimum-description-length term that trades compression against reuse.
numbers: BabyAI zero-shot average success: LAST 43, LISA 36, LOVE 37, BC 34. BossLevel 36 vs BC 25. Largest ALFRED gain on GoTo tasks. Removing the MDL term lowers performance.
limits: Needs expert demonstrations and training. Gains are modest (6-9 points on the BabyAI average).
agent_relevance: Supports compression pressure as a way to pick good subgoals: a skill must be both short and reused. Can be copied as a library admission rule.

source: Czechowski et al. (2021) Subgoal Search For Complex Reasoning Tasks (kSubS)
finding: A learned generator proposes subgoals k steps ahead, and search runs over subgoals rather than single actions. State of the art on INT inequality proving, large gains on Rubik's cube and Sokoban.
numbers: Rubik's cube: BF-kSubS solves nearly 100%, best-first on primitive moves under 10%. Sokoban at graph size 50: 12x12 0.66 vs 0.15, 16x16 0.42 vs 0.04, 20x20 0.46 vs 0.02 (kSubS vs best-first). About 65% of generated Sokoban subgoals reduce distance; 17% increase it. About 50% of INT and Rubik's subgoals are reachable by the low-level policy and the rest are discarded.
limits: Generators are trained on solved data. My text extraction garbled some table cells, so only the clear cells are quoted.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that subgoal search beats action search. Design rule: check that each proposed subgoal is reachable and discard those that are not.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Prompting the model to list easier sub-problems first and solve them in order gives large gains on tasks longer than the examples, but small gains on GSM8K.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: 99.7% least-to-most vs 16.2-16.7% chain-of-thought. Last-letter concatenation, length 12: 74.0% vs 31.8%. GSM8K overall 62.39% vs 60.97%; problems needing 5+ steps 45.23% vs 39.07%.
limits: Decomposition prompts are task-specific. Almost every GSM8K failure is solved with a manual decomposition, so the model-written decomposition is the weak part.
agent_relevance: Decomposition quality is the bottleneck. A model-written subgoal list is only as good as its decomposer, so check it with code or a library.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench
finding: On classical Blocksworld planning, plain LLMs plan poorly, and several auxiliary tasks that look easier are also weak.
numbers: GPT-4: plan generation 206/600 (34.3%), cost-optimal planning 198/600 (33%), plan verification 191/600 (31.8%). InstructGPT-3 plan generation 41/600 (6.8%).
limits: Blocksworld has little hierarchical structure. One domain, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Baseline for what a bare LLM does on multi-step planning. Supports handing subgoal bookkeeping to code.

source: Machado et al. (2018) deep SR eigenoptions, end states
finding: The paper notes that Kulkarni et al. (2016) suggested a deep SR could find bottleneck states. In Atari the greedy myopic options sit at their end state, so visitation mass piles up at one screen location.
numbers: Atari: Bank Heist, Freeway, Montezuma's Revenge, Ms. Pac-Man; options useful in 3 of 4.
limits: Qualitative visitation plots, no head-to-head reward numbers in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Validation was by eye. For us, a subgoal needs a code-checkable end condition, not a vague direction.

source: Machado et al. (2023) JMLR, option keyboard
finding: The SR also supports combining options through the option keyboard: new options are made as linear mixes of base ones (Section 8 of the paper).
numbers: No numbers quoted.
limits: I read the framing only, not the keyboard experiments.
agent_relevance: Suggests a library of a few base subgoals that compose, rather than many one-off ones.

source: Machado et al. (2023) JMLR, covering options
finding: Covering options (single-state initiation sets) did not help reward learning in any of 10 four-room tasks, while eigenoptions did. The authors guess the sparse initiation set is the reason. Earlier work had only measured them by diffusion time.
numbers: 10 tasks, 50 episodes, 1,000-step cap.
limits: One domain. The explanation is a conjecture.
agent_relevance: An option available in few states is rarely used. Prefer subgoals with wide applicability.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT, different LLMs
finding: ADaPT improves GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA and Lemur on all three datasets (figure only; per-model numbers not extracted).
numbers: Abstract headline: up to 28.3% higher in ALFWorld, 27% in WebShop, 33% in TextCraft than strong baselines.
limits: Chat variants of GPT-3.5 underperformed the completion model, so the completion one was used.
agent_relevance: The gain holds across model sizes, so a scaffold that decomposes on failure is not model-specific.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, ablations
finding: Six design choices were ablated, including automatic curriculum, skill library and feedback types. Each removal lowered the discovered-item count; self-verification mattered most.
numbers: -73% items without self-verification. Tech-tree cells are fractions out of 3 runs.
limits: Only 3 runs per cell. No confidence intervals in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: Order of importance for a library loop: verify before admitting, then curriculum, then retrieval.

source: Czechowski et al. (2021) kSubS, subgoal distance k
finding: Subgoal distance has a sweet spot. Too short gives little saving. Too long makes the generator less accurate and the low-level policy harder.
numbers: Best k = 3 on INT and 4 on Rubik's cube; larger k degraded results.
limits: Domain-specific k.
agent_relevance: Subgoal grain matters. Test two or three grain sizes on our own tasks.

source: Czechowski et al. (2021) kSubS, generalisation and budget
finding: Subgoal search trained on length-10 proofs generalises to longer proofs. It also gives up to 7x faster execution in some settings.
numbers: INT proof length 5: baseline transformer over 99%. Sokoban expert data solves 78/67/60% by board size, and kSubS beats this already at graph size 1000.
limits: The authors only speculate that search causes the out-of-distribution effect.
agent_relevance: Planning over subgoals is a route to problems longer than the examples.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most, exemplar control
finding: Chain-of-thought with more exemplars improves but still lags least-to-most on long lists.
numbers: Length-12 lists: CoT 37.4% with 4 exemplars, 38.4% with 8; least-to-most 74.0%.
limits: Extra exemplars do not match the extra tokens of decomposition exactly.
agent_relevance: The gain is not only prompt length.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval, discussion
finding: The authors suggest LLMs need memory and executive-control add-ons, and name schemas (generalised cognitive maps) and multi-scale planning as next steps.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Discussion, not a tested result.
agent_relevance: Authors of the neuroscience-side evaluation also point to hierarchical structure plus a scaffold as the likely fix.

source: Du et al. (2023) ELLM, comparison to novelty rewards
finding: ELLM usually matches or beats novelty methods (RND, APT, Novelty) on downstream tasks, but the gain varies by task and seed.
numbers: Seven downstream Crafter tasks plus Housekeep rearrangement tasks; per-task values not extracted.
limits: The authors note high seed-to-seed variance.
agent_relevance: LLM priors beat pure novelty when the goal space is large, and are weaker when common sense is irrelevant.

source: Machado et al. (2018) deep SR, myopia
finding: The authors link the missed key subgoal in Montezuma and the Freeway failure to a greedy myopic option policy, not to the SR itself.
numbers: One of four games failed.
limits: Explanation offered, not tested.
agent_relevance: A subgoal found by structure still needs a planner that looks ahead to use it.
